name: Voya
tagline: Group travel with a shared pot powered by stablecoins
intro: Every group trip starts the same way: a group chat, a lot of excitement, and somebody quietly volunteering to be the one who keeps track of the money. Voya is my attempt to make sure nobody has to be that person again.

sections.heading: The problem with group trips
paragraphs: Planning a trip with friends is mostly coordination. Where are we going, what are we doing each day, how much is this going to cost, and who has paid for what so far. The fun part, actually going, sits on top of a pile of spreadsheets, screenshots and “I’ll send it to you later” messages.
The money is where it usually gets awkward. One person books the accommodation, another covers dinner, someone else pays for the tickets, and by the end of the trip nobody is quite sure who owes who.

sections.heading: What Voya does
paragraphs: Voya takes a trip from daydream to departure. It builds the itinerary, works out the budget, and makes splitting the cost painless.

Instead of settling up after the fact, friends pool money into a shared pot before the trip. Everyone can see what has gone in and what has gone out, and the pot pays for the things the group agreed on.

sections.heading: Why stablecoins
paragraphs: The shared pot runs on stablecoins behind the scenes. Friends don’t need to think about that part; they just see a pot of money in a currency they understand. Stablecoins handle the rest, which matters a lot when the people in a group live in different places and use different currencies.
It’s the same idea that runs through most of my fintech work: the technology should do the heavy lifting quietly, and the person using it should only see something simple.

sections.heading: Where it is now
paragraphs: Voya is in active development and the waitlist is open. If you’re the friend who always ends up planning the trip, I’m building this for you.

name: General Intelligence Labs
tagline: Three friends from uni building AI-native products, one venture at a time
intro: General Intelligence Labs is three friends who keep building things together: Christian, Eugene and me. We take our ventures seriously and ourselves a little less so, which is how one of our long-running goals became, half-jokingly, to one day post that we’ve raised $100M to change the future of QA.

sections.heading: How we met
paragraphs: I met Christian and Eugene at university, when they were both in Level 400. They are two of the smartest people I know.
Eugene and I went on to spend over a year on the engineering team at Polymorph Labs together, even though we worked on different teams for most of that time.

sections.heading: Integrion: AI-native QA
paragraphs: Our first venture, in 2024, was Integrion: AI-native QA engineering for distributed systems. The goal was to build the go-to AI-powered automated QA tool for backend systems.
We fell into our roles naturally, and they have mostly stuck. I owned the frontend, Eugene owned the backend, and Christian owned the AI.
We got to demo Integrion in some cool places, including Google. In the end, we couldn’t keep up with the cost of AI credits, and we closed it down.

sections.heading: Athena, now Liuca: the AI-native accountant
paragraphs: After a long break, we came back with our next venture: an AI-native accountant. We built out the MVP and were getting ready to launch when a multi-million-dollar financial company released their own version.

That felt surreal. They obviously had deeper pockets and more reach. Instead of giving up, we took some time, learned from what they shipped, and refined our product. It was called Athena; it’s now called Liuca, and it’s ready for use.

sections.heading: Agentic spending on stablecoin rails
paragraphs: We like being at the edge of what AI can do, and a couple of months ago we started looking at a frontier not many people were considering yet: agentic spending, where AI agents can spend money on your behalf, within limits you control.

For the WeWire Hackhive 2.0, we built controlled agentic spending on stablecoin rails. We didn’t win. The feedback, more or less, was that our solution was too advanced to be a viable startup in the African market right now. We like to think we were just ahead of our time, especially since some of the biggest names in stablecoins are now working on the same idea.

sections.heading: Ovaal: an agentic cashier for restaurants
paragraphs: Our most recent venture is a partnership with Forge Studios, the engineering and design studio in Accra, Ghana. Together we’re building an agentic cashier for restaurants, integrated into Ovaal, Forge’s restaurant POS system.
We recently tested V1. It went quite well, and we’re actively refining it.

name: Quotient
tagline: A limit order book and matching engine with price-time priority, the core of how exchanges execute orders
intro: Quotient is a limit order book and matching engine. It implements price-time priority matching: the mechanism exchanges and trading venues use to decide which orders trade, at what price, and in what order.

sections.heading: What it does
paragraphs: It takes limit orders, which buy or sell at a set price or better, and market orders, which execute immediately at the best available price. Matching follows price-time priority: the best price trades first, and among equal prices the earliest order wins.

Orders can fill partially across several resting orders, and they can be cancelled or modified. Every execution goes into a trade log, and the book can be queried for its depth: the total quantity waiting at each price level.

sections.heading: How it’s built
paragraphs: Each side of the book is a map from price to a first-in, first-out queue of orders at that price. Heaps over the price levels (a max-heap for bids, a min-heap for asks) give constant-time reads of the best bid and ask, and logarithmic-time updates.

The engine and its REST API are written in TypeScript and tested with Vitest. I also ported the order book and matching engine to C++, purely to benchmark throughput and latency against the TypeScript version.

sections.heading: Trading against live prices
paragraphs: An optional adapter feeds real market data in: it consumes the IEX stock feed through Alpaca’s WebSocket API and turns quotes into liquidity the engine can trade against.
On top sits a React paper-trading workstation with order entry, a clickable depth ladder, a session price trace, and time and sales.

name: Stackd
tagline: A platform for creators and brands: opportunities, submissions, wallets and payouts
intro: Stackd is a platform I’m building for creators and brands. It’s split into three apps: a core backend that runs the platform, an app for creators, and an app for brands.

sections.heading: The core platform
paragraphs: The core is a GraphQL API built with Apollo Server on Express, backed by Postgres on Neon through Drizzle ORM. It’s organised into modules for opportunities, submissions, payments, wallets, KYC, disputes, messaging, notifications, social features and admin.

Background work such as notifications runs on BullMQ queues over Redis. Email goes out through Resend, push notifications through Firebase Cloud Messaging, and media is handled by Cloudinary. Payments come in through Paystack, and the whole service ships as a Docker container.

sections.heading: The creators app
paragraphs: Creators get a TanStack Start app running on Cloudflare Workers. It talks to the core over GraphQL with Apollo Client and covers sign-up, onboarding and a dashboard.
It’s built with Tailwind and Radix-based components, with Sentry for error monitoring and PostHog for product analytics.

sections.heading: The brand app
paragraphs: A third app, for brands, completes the platform alongside the core and the creators app.

name: UpStack
tagline: A distributed, content-addressable object storage system with delta sync and shared folders
intro: UpStack is a distributed, content-addressable storage system. It keeps file metadata strongly consistent while letting the bulk object data be eventually consistent, by separating metadata management from where the bytes are physically stored.

sections.heading: How files are stored
paragraphs: Files are split into fixed 4 MB blocks, and each block is identified by its SHA-256 hash. Because blocks are addressed by their content, identical data is only ever stored once.
Before uploading, a client asks the server which of its block hashes it doesn’t have yet, and only sends those. Changing part of a large file means re-sending only the blocks that changed.

sections.heading: Staying in sync
paragraphs: A sync agent written in Go watches local folders and uploads changes automatically, with no user action needed.

Every metadata commit increments a version number. The server uses optimistic concurrency control: if a client tries to commit against a version that’s already been superseded, it gets a 409 Conflict instead of overwriting someone else’s changes.

sections.heading: Sharing and the console
paragraphs: Each file has a fixed owner, who can share it with other people by email. A React management console handles uploads, downloads, shared files and permissions.
The backend is written in Go, with MongoDB for metadata, S3 or local disk for objects, JWT authentication and bcrypt-hashed passwords.

name: Explainable AI Backend
tagline: An API that turns machine learning models and datasets into human-readable explanations
intro: Machine learning models are good at making predictions and bad at explaining them. This backend takes a model and its data and returns explanations people can actually read: charts, plus a narrative of what drove each prediction.

sections.heading: What it explains
paragraphs: It supports three explanation methods: SHAP, LIME and Integrated Gradients. It works with tabular, text and image models, can explain a single row or a whole batch, and returns narrative-rich JSON and HTML reports alongside the plots.
It’s built to be extended, so new models and explanation methods can be plugged in.

sections.heading: How it’s built
paragraphs: The API is written in Python with FastAPI, using SHAP, LIME and Captum for the explanations and Matplotlib and Plotly for the charts. It works with scikit-learn, XGBoost, LightGBM, PyTorch and TensorFlow models.
It can be used through the API or a command-line tool, and it’s containerised with Docker and Docker Compose. The API docs are live at explainable-backend.onrender.com/docs.

name: VoteMaster
tagline: A GraphQL voting engine for organisations, events, categories and nominees
intro: VoteMaster is the backend engine for a voting platform. Organisations run events, each event is split into categories, and each category has nominees.

sections.heading: How it’s built
paragraphs: It’s a GraphQL API built with Apollo Server on Express, with the schema split into modules for authentication, events and categories.
Data lives in MongoDB through Mongoose, with models for organisations, events, categories and nominees. Authentication uses JSON Web Tokens, and passwords are hashed with bcrypt.

name: DNS Server
tagline: A DNS server written from scratch in TypeScript, answering queries over UDP
intro: DNS is how a name like google.com becomes an IP address. I built a DNS server from scratch in TypeScript through CodeCrafters’ “Build your own DNS server” challenge, working directly with the raw binary messages.

sections.heading: Speaking DNS
paragraphs: The server listens for queries over UDP. For each one, it reads the header (transaction ID, flags and question count), then parses the domain name from DNS’s length-prefixed label format with its own parser, followed by the query type and class.
It then builds the response byte by byte in a 512-byte buffer, encoding the header, question and answer records, and answers from a small in-memory set of records.

name: Circuit Breaker
tagline: A lightweight, configurable circuit breaker that keeps Node.js services resilient
intro: When a service you depend on starts failing, calling it again and again only makes things worse. A circuit breaker notices the failures, stops the calls for a while, and lets the service recover. This is a lightweight, customisable one for Node.js.

sections.heading: How it works
paragraphs: The breaker starts closed, letting calls through. When failures reach a threshold, it opens and rejects calls immediately instead of waiting on a broken service.

After a timeout it goes half-open and lets a trial call through. If enough trial calls succeed, it closes again. The failure threshold, success threshold and timeout are all configurable; the defaults are 5 failures, 1 success and 5 seconds.

sections.heading: Using it
paragraphs: Any async action can be wrapped in the breaker. The repo includes examples for a basic case, an HTTP API called with axios, and a database call, with tests written in Mocha and Chai.

name: Custom-Built CLI
tagline: A command-line tool built with Node.js
intro: A command-line tool built with Node.js. It installs as its own command, parses arguments with arg, and prints coloured output with chalk.

sections.heading: How it’s built
paragraphs: Commands and configuration live in separate modules, so new commands can be added without touching the rest. The repo includes a test project to run the tool against.
